I wish there were a switch you could just flip to turn it off. But the truth is, you can’t completely stop caring—and honestly, you probably wouldn't want to, because caring deeply is also tied to your ability to love, be empathetic, and be a good friend. 

The goal isn't to become cold or numb; it’s to stop letting other people's opinions—or your *assumptions* of their opinions—dictate whether you feel okay as a person.

It’s a slow practice, but here are a few things that actually help take the power back:

### 1. Stop doing the work of rejecting yourself for them
When you don't hear back, your brain fills in the blank with: *"They're sick of me."* You are essentially rejecting yourself on their behalf before they’ve even said a word. Try to catch yourself and make a rule: **I will only respond to what people actually tell me, not the story my fear is writing.** If they have an issue, it is *their* responsibility as an adult to communicate it. 

### 2. Flip the question
When you care too much what others think, your brain is constantly asking: 
* *"Did I say the right thing?"*
* *"Do they still like me?"*
* *"Am I being annoying?"*

Try flipping the focus back to *you*:
* *"Do I like how this person makes me feel?"*
* *"Did I speak my truth honestly in that message?"*
* *"Is this friendship giving me the safety and reciprocity I need?"*

You spend so much energy worrying if you are good enough for them, you forget to ask if the dynamic is actually good for *you*.

### 3. Make peace with being "too much" for some people
This is the hardest one. You have to accept that you might send a message that is too long, too emotional, or too intense for *some* people. And that’s okay. It doesn't mean the message was bad; it just means it exceeded *their* capacity. If you have to shrink yourself, edit your thoughts to the bone, and walk on eggshells to keep someone around, you aren't actually keeping them—you're just keeping an illusion alive.

### 4. Give people permission to misunderstand you
You cannot control what someone thinks of you, no matter how carefully you craft a text or how low-maintenance you try to be. When the urge comes to reread the text and "fix" it in your head, try telling yourself: *"I said what I said. They might love it, they might be overwhelmed by it, they might take a week to reply. But I release control over how they receive it."*

It takes time to rewire this, especially if you've been hurt before. But you deserve to take up space without feeling like you have to apologize for existing.
